motive: User asked whether operator equivalence can move the ASR encoder onto the NPU. Re-examining the 2026-10-08 conclusion.

sourceGraph.note: fully rewritten graph from rewrite_asr_encoder_npu_ops.py; all four HiAI operator refusals already removed

findings.step: Is the capacity wall weight bytes or node count?
findings.method: Same 749-node prefix converted at fp16 (20,670,200 B) and fp32 (40,785,400 B); both built on NNRt.

evidence.contrast: At fp16 the 750th node is refused at only 20.5 MB, while 749 nodes at 40.8 MB are accepted. A byte cap is ruled out by contradiction.

findings.consequence: Node/operator count is the binding constraint, so node-count reduction is the only lever a graph rewrite has.

findings.method: fp16 prefixes at 800, 900, 1200 nodes on NNRt.

findings.step: Does the converter's own transformer fusion shrink the graph?
findings.method: Full graph converted with --optimizeTransformer=true vs false.

evidence.meaning: zipformer2 uses relative-position attention plus nonlin-attention, which MindSpore Lite's BERT-style fusion rules do not match.

findings.step: Can the 7-node stable softplus be replaced by the single ONNX Softplus op?
findings.method: Micro-model MatMul(512x512) -> Softplus -> Sub on NNRt, with an identical control that omits only Softplus.
findings.consequence: The 95-site 7-node rewrite is necessary, not gratuitous. It costs ~495 nodes that cannot be reclaimed.

findings.step: How much node-count headroom is left for operator equivalence?
findings.method: Static count of remaining fusable patterns in the rewritten graph.
findings.consequence: Whole-graph single-model offload is unreachable by operator equivalence. The compute core alone is 521 nodes, and the rest is structural.

findings.step: Split the encoder into sequential sub-models under the wall
findings.method: Six slices of 628 nodes (last 626) cut with make_slice.py using inferred static shapes; each converted to MindIR fp16 and built on NNRt.
findings.result: ALL SIX ACCEPTED ON THE NPU

evidence.excludes: inter-slice host-side tensor plumbing (19-31 tensors, 0.6-1.3 MiB per boundary)

findings.consequence: The 2026-10-08 claim that the ASR encoder cannot be moved to the NPU is wrong. The per-model capacity wall is bypassed by splitting.

findings.step: Re-measure the NPU/CPU latency ratio that the earlier 'not worth it' verdict rested on
findings.method: Same prefixes at 200/400/600/749 nodes, both backends, 7 iterations each, back to back on a warm device.

evidence.whyEarlierNumberDiffered: The NPU side reproduces (749-node min 32.51 ms today vs 33.96 ms on 2026-10-08). The CPU side moved: min 30.08 ms today vs 18.77 ms then. The earlier ratio was taken against a cold-CPU baseline; a warm device, which is the condition this whole effort is about, removes the gap.

findings.consequence: The 1.59-1.70x figure is not a stable property. It must not be used as the reason to reject the split.

findings.step: Does the six-slice chain compute the same function as the single graph?
findings.method: onnxruntime 1.24.3 on the host: run the rewritten graph once on random inputs, then run the six slices in sequence, feeding each slice the graph inputs plus the frontier tensors produced by earlier slices, and recover all graph outputs.
findings.consequence: Splitting does not change the mathematics. The 117 cached-state and encoder outputs are produced across all six slices, so the host must collect outputs from every slice, not only the last.

findings.step: Process CPU cost per backend for identical work
findings.method: Probe the same slice (628-1256) with iterations=1 and iterations=100 on each backend and difference /proc/<pid>/stat utime+stime, so the one app start cancels and 99 inferences remain. The probe caps iterations at 100, so longer loops are not available.
findings.result: NPU USES 16.1% OF THE CPU TIME
findings.consequence: The trade is 6.2x less CPU time for 1.62x more wall time. That is the direction that matters for heat: the thermal matrix established that heat tracks CPU bursts and that ASR is a flat ~1.8-core load.

findings.step: Steady-state cost of the whole six-slice chain on the NPU
findings.method: Each slice probed with iterations=100 (thread pools and the accelerator warm), plus per-slice CPU tick differencing as in R9.

evidence.excludes: host-side plumbing of 19-31 boundary tensors per slice (0.6-1.3 MiB each)

findings.consequence: Real-time with margin, at under a tenth of a core of host CPU for the encoder. Note the 7-iteration numbers taken earlier are cold: the MindSpore Lite CPU backend's median for slice 628-1256 fell from 20.49 ms to 10.68 ms once warm, which is a second reason the 2026-10-08 ratio was unreliable.

findings.step: Equivalence of the ten-slice, byte-aware partition
findings.method: Same host check as R8, on the partition that respects both the NPU node wall (<=700) and a per-slice fp16 weight budget (<=35 MB).

findings.step: MindSpore Lite CPU backend cannot host the weight-dense middle of the encoder
findings.method: All ten slices built on both backends.

evidence.note: The refused five are the 768-dim layers: few nodes (203-230) but ~35 MB of weights each. The process is killed with no fault log. Size alone does not explain it: 2952-3519 is 36.8 MB and loads.

findings.consequence: A same-runtime CPU control arm can only cover the 2484 of 3766 nodes (66%) that both backends accept.

findings.step: Paired thermal A/B of the encoder chain, NPU versus MindSpore Lite CPU
findings.method: New paced chain probe (probeMindSporeChain): builds the five commonly-accepted slices once, then runs all five in order once per 640 ms tick (the real decode_chunk_len=64 cadence) for 960 s. Each arm cooled first to a stable baseline; thermal zones and /proc/<pid>/stat sampled every 10 s.
findings.result: CPU TIME: 10.8x LESS ON NPU. TEMPERATURE: NO MEASURABLE DIFFERENCE.

evidence.temperatureVerdict: Not discriminating. By endpoint samples the NPU arm rose 0.10 C and the CPU arm 0.30 C, but by first-third versus last-third means it is 0.069 C against 0.009 C, i.e. the sign reverses. The NPU arm's own within-arm range is 0.668 C, larger than any between-arm difference. Neither arm produced a measurable rise in 960 s.

findings.consequence: The mechanism is confirmed and large: offloading removes about 91% of the encoder's host CPU cost and, at steady state over 16 minutes, is also 1.41x faster in wall time with zero pacing overruns. The heat question is NOT answered: in isolation at the real duty cycle the encoder does not heat this device measurably on either backend, starting near 30 C with 24.6 C ambient. The product reaches 40-45 C only because the whole pipeline runs 1.8-2.4 cores alongside screen, microphone and radio, and that is where power scales nonlinearly. A product-level thermal answer requires the encoder actually substituted inside sherpa's call path, not a synthetic arm.

findings.step: Production baseline: the delivered INT8 encoder on ONNX Runtime
findings.method: New diagnostics-only ORT probe (probeOrtModel) in the same carrier: loads the shipped encoder.int8.onnx with 4 intra-op threads, the thread count the engine uses, and times Run on zero-filled inputs. CPU time by differencing /proc/<pid>/stat across a 1-iteration and a 30-iteration run so the one app start and model load cancel.
findings.result: THE REAL BASELINE IS 3.3x CHEAPER IN CPU THAN THE MINDSPORE LITE FP16 CPU BACKEND

model.note: matches the md5 pinned in the 0.3.21 release BUILD_PROVENANCE, i.e. the shipped weights

mindsporeLiteFp16CpuForContrast.note: fp16 on MindSpore Lite is not the product path; comparing against it overstated the saving

findings.consequence: Every earlier CPU-side ratio in this record was measured against the wrong baseline and must be read as a mechanism check, not as product economics.

findings.step: The candidate against the real baseline
findings.method: Full ten-slice chain on the NPU driven by the paced probe at the real 640 ms chunk cadence; CPU time by the same 1-tick versus 60 s differencing.
findings.result: 2.67x SLOWER IN WALL TIME FOR A 59% CPU-TIME SAVING
findings.consequence: Substituting the encoder removes at most 16.2 of the 181.0 single-core-equivalent points that ASR-only was measured to draw, about 9% of its CPU load, while making the encoder 2.67x slower per chunk (RTF 0.084 -> 0.225) and adding 308 MB of MindIR assets plus 3.8 s of model build on load and ten-model boundary plumbing. For contrast, the speaker encoder migration that shipped removed 31.0-36.6 CPU points and 2.07-2.78 C. The isolated thermal A/B could not detect a temperature difference at a larger CPU delta than this one.

findings.method: MindSpore Lite weight quantisation (quant_type=WEIGHT_QUANT, bit_num=8) on shaped prefixes and on individual slices, with and without [registry] disable_fusion.

evidence.error: legacy_optimizer/graph/infershape_pass.cc:633 InferShape failed, name: /chunkwise_conv_*/Conv, type: Conv2DFusion; then InferSubgraph index: 0 failed, ret: -500
evidence.failingOps: 1-D depthwise convolutions: input rank 3, kernel_shape [31] or [16], group=256
evidence.cause: The quantisation path forces MindSpore Lite's legacy infershape pass, which --infer=false skips for the fp16 path. That pass maps ONNX Conv to Conv2DFusion and cannot infer a rank-3 1-D convolution. disable_fusion does not help: Conv2DFusion is the parser's canonical op name, not a fusion result.
evidence.knownWorkaround: Lift the 1-D convolutions to 2-D with reshape pairs, the technique already used for pooling in rewrite_asr_encoder_npu_ops.py. Not pursued: it adds about two nodes per convolution across 82 convolutions, pushing a node count already 4.5x over the wall further over it, and its only payoff is halving asset bytes, which R1 showed is not the binding constraint.

stillUnknown: Whether the product gets cooler. Unanswered, and now unlikely to be worth answering: the isolated encoder at real cadence does not heat this device measurably on either backend, and the CPU delta against the real baseline is 16.2 points of 181.0.
A product-level thermal A/B would still need the encoder substituted inside sherpa. That work is not done and is not recommended on these numbers.
The MindSpore Lite CPU backend cannot host the weight-dense middle five slices at all (process killed, no fault log), so no same-runtime CPU control exists for the full graph.
int8 MindIR is blocked by the converter's legacy infershape pass on 1-D depthwise convolutions; the workaround is known but costs nodes for no benefit that bears on the wall.
toolingAdded: make_slice.py (node-range slice extraction with inferred static shapes)
revisedConclusion: The ASR encoder CAN be moved to this device's NPU - as ten sequential MindIR sub-models under a per-model node wall of about 750, bit-exact against the single graph - so the 2026-10-08 claim that it cannot was wrong, and so was the 1.59-1.70x latency ratio it was rejected on. But measured against the baseline that actually ships, the delivered INT8 encoder on ORT with 4 threads, the trade is poor: 143.85 ms against 53.80 ms per 640 ms chunk (2.67x slower, encoder RTF 0.084 -> 0.225) for 72.4 against 175.9 CPU-ms (a 59% CPU-time saving worth at most 16.2 of the 181.0 single-core-equivalent points ASR-only draws, about 9% of its CPU load). Add 308 MB of MindIR assets, 3.8 s of model build on load, and ten-model boundary plumbing across two runtimes inside sherpa's encoder path. The isolated thermal A/B could not detect a temperature difference at a larger CPU delta than this. The recommendation is not to integrate: the heat lever that measured well is flattening diarization bursts, not moving the ASR encoder.
